title: Babur on irrigation in northern India
body: In his memoirs, the Babur Nama, the first Mughal emperor described how fields and orchards were watered in northern India. In Lahore and Dipalpur, he wrote, people made two circles of rope long enough for the depth of the well, fixed strips of wood between them and fastened pitchers on these. The ropes with the pitchers were put over a wheel-well. A second wheel was fixed on the axle and another on an upright axle; the bullock turned the last wheel, whose teeth caught in the teeth of the second, so that the wheel with the pitchers turned and emptied water into a trough. In Agra, Chandwar and Bayana, people instead set up a fork of wood at the well-edge with a roller between the forks, tied a rope to a large bucket, passed it over the roller and tied its other end to a bullock. One person had to drive the bullock and another had to empty the bucket.

title: The Ain on collecting revenue in kind
body: The Ain-i Akbari instructed the amil-guzar (revenue collector) not to take revenue only in cash but also in kind, which could be done in several ways. Under kankut (kan meaning grain and kut meaning estimate), the crop was estimated; if doubts arose, crops were cut and estimated in three lots - good, middling and inferior. Under batai, also called bhaoli, the crops were reaped, stacked and divided by agreement in the presence of the parties, which required several intelligent inspectors to prevent deception. Under khet-batai, the fields were divided after they were sown. Under lang batai, the grain was cut, formed into heaps and divided, and each party took its share home.
